analysis.one_liner: Lets banks buy other banks and open branches in any state, overriding state limits.
analysis.headline: Introduced by one Democrat with one Republican cosponsor, the bill got two subcommittee hearings in 1993 but was never brought to a vote and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let bank holding companies buy banks in any state even where state law said no, and let national banks, state banks, and foreign banks open branches across state lines. States could keep out-of-state branches only if they passed a ban within a short two-year window after the bill became law. In exchange, federal regulators would have to review big banks' lending records state by state and write rules ensuring each interstate branch served its local community.
analysis.who_benefits: Large bank holding companies and foreign banks, which could acquire banks and open branches nationwide instead of negotiating state-by-state. Some consumers might gain convenience and more branch options, and communities would get new federal reviews of banks' local lending records.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large bank holding companies and foreign banks

how_it_helps.text: Would let the Federal Reserve approve a bank holding company's acquisition of a bank in any state, 'notwithstanding any State law' that would prohibit or limit it, repealing the old requirement that states expressly authorize such deals [S2][S3].

Would let national banks open or buy branches in other states with Comptroller of the Currency approval, and insured state banks do the same if their home state allows it, after a two-year transition [S2][S3].

Would require federal banking agencies to write a separate Community Reinvestment Act evaluation of a bank's lending record for every state where it has branches, and to issue rules ensuring each interstate branch meets local credit needs [S2][S3].

Would let states opt out only by enacting, within two years of enactment, a law that bans all out-of-state banks' branches equally; a state that bans branching could later change its mind and allow it [S3].

analysis.who_pays: States that wanted to keep decisions about out-of-state banking local would lose that authority, since federal approval would override state acquisition laws. Small local banks would face takeovers by and competition from nationwide giants. Communities could see lending decisions consolidated away from local institutions, mitigated only by the bill's new CRA review rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: State banking authority and small local banks

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state laws restricting out-of-state bank takeovers and gives states only a two-year window to enact a ban on interstate branching, a short time for state legislatures to act [S3].

Making interstate acquisitions and branching routine by default would tilt the playing field toward large nationwide banks over community banks, since out-of-state companies could buy up local institutions without state-level consent; the bill's protections for local credit depend on regulators writing and enforcing strong CRA rules [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Banking across state lines had real consumer appeal — more branches, more competition, and the bill adds genuine safeguards by requiring state-by-state lending reviews. But its core move is federal preemption of state banking laws with a narrow opt-out window, which mainly advantages large banking companies and weakens local control over who owns local banks. How well ordinary depositors and borrowers fared would depend heavily on the CRA regulations the bill delegates to federal agencies.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Banking Committee's financial institutions subcommittee after two hearings and was never voted on by the subcommittee, the full committee, or the House before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Peter Hoagland introduced the bill on January 6, 1993, joined by Representative McCollum, its one cosponsor [S1][S3][S4][S5].

The House referred it to the Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs on the day of introduction, and on February 1, 1993 it went to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions Supervision, Regulation and Deposit Insurance [S5].
The subcommittee held hearings on June 22 and July 29, 1993, but no markup or vote followed [S5].
No further action was taken before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, state restrictions on out-of-state bank acquisitions and branching stayed in place for the rest of that Congress, as did the role of community banks and state regulators. Large banking companies got nothing from this bill itself, though Congress enacted similar nationwide banking and branching legislation the following year in the Riegle-Neal Act of 1994.

against.name: House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Financial Institutions Subcommittee on February 1, 1993; no full-committee markup or vote was ever scheduled during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no partisan split is recorded; the sponsor was a Democrat with a single Republican cosponsor, and the bill died in a Democratic-controlled committee without action.

industries.note: The bill's central purpose was to let big banking companies acquire banks and open branches in any state, overriding state laws that limited them. Its interest in preemption ran against the state-level control and local banking alternatives that critics of interstate banking sought to preserve, though the bill attached state-by-state CRA lending reviews as a concession to communities.

industries.industry: Community banks and small local banks
industries.note: Out-of-state companies could buy local banks without state consent, exposing small institutions to takeover and competition from nationwide banks. Their fortunes are tied to local branch presence and local lending relationships.

industries.industry: State banking regulators and state authority
industries.note: Federal approval would override state acquisition laws, and states would have only a two-year window to opt out of interstate branching. States would retain taxation and some examination powers, but their core gatekeeping role would shrink.

The bill would prescribe guidelines letting foreign banks establish interstate branches and agencies on terms equivalent to domestic banks, expanding their U.S. footprint subject to capital-equivalency tests.
